lesson.title: Network Namespaces: One Kernel, Many Isolated Networks
lesson.summary: A Linux network namespace is an isolated copy of the network stack, its own interfaces, routing table, and firewall rules, that lets one machine host many logically separate networks, the mechanism underneath container networking.
lesson.body:
A computer network is built from hosts, each with its own addresses, interfaces, and routing decisions about where to send a packet next. Normally, that description applies once per physical machine: one machine, one network stack, one set of interfaces and routes. Network namespaces break that assumption. A network namespace is a Linux kernel feature that creates an isolated network stack, complete with its own loopback interface, its own set of network interfaces, its own routing table, and its own firewall rules, so that a single physical machine can behave like many independent hosts at once.

The reason this matters is containers. A container is supposed to look, from the inside, like its own isolated machine, with its own IP address and its own view of the network, even though it is really just a process running on a shared kernel alongside dozens of other containers. Network namespaces are the specific piece of Linux that makes that illusion real for networking: each container gets its own namespace, so processes inside it cannot see or interfere with another container's interfaces or routes, and a process listening on port 80 inside one container's namespace does not conflict with another process listening on port 80 inside a different one.

A freshly created network namespace starts completely isolated. It has a loopback interface and nothing else, no way to reach the outside world and no way for the outside world to reach it. To connect it to anything, you typically create a veth pair, a virtual Ethernet cable with two ends, place one end inside the namespace and leave the other end outside, in the host's default namespace or another namespace. You can build and test this directly:

  ip netns add ns1
  ip netns add ns2
  ip link add veth1 type veth peer name veth2
  ip link set veth1 netns ns1
  ip link set veth2 netns ns2
  ip netns exec ns1 ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev veth1
  ip netns exec ns2 ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev veth2
  ip netns exec ns1 ip link set veth1 up
  ip netns exec ns1 ip link set lo up
  ip netns exec ns2 ip link set veth2 up
  ip netns exec ns2 ip link set lo up
  ip netns exec ns1 ping -c 3 10.0.0.2

This creates two fully isolated network stacks on a single machine and connects them with a single virtual cable, and the ping succeeds because the veth pair behaves exactly like two hosts wired directly together. This is a small-scale version of exactly what container runtimes like Docker do automatically: each container is given its own network namespace, and a veth pair connects it out to the host, usually into a shared virtual switch rather than a single point-to-point link, which is precisely the problem the Linux bridge solves once you have more than two namespaces to connect.
